about: A way across country, told as it goes, a sentence or two and no more: setting out (by the hour and the sky: fair, grey, rain, fog, wind, cold, hot, ash), the land the way runs through (by what its cells are: water crossed, fen, wood, open fields, moor, a pass), the light going on the way, and coming in sight of where it ends (by the size of the settlement). {from} and {to} are where the way begins and ends; {way} is what it is, a road or a path (a track over the fells is not a road). When every line that fits has been said, the one said longest ago is said again.

lines.text: You leave {from} with the sun low behind you and the dew still on the grass.
You set out from {from} early, with your shadow long in front of you on the {way}.
You leave {from} in the full of the morning, with the sun climbing and the {way} dry underfoot.
You leave {from} in a white fog that turns the hedges to ghosts at ten paces.
You leave {from} with your hood up and the rain in your face.
It rains on and off the whole way, the soft rain that gets in everywhere.
Rain comes over in grey curtains, one after another, and between them the country shines.
You set out from {from} in the middle of the afternoon, and the rain sets out with you.
You leave {from} late, in rain, with the light going early under the cloud.
It is cold enough to see your breath, and the ruts are hard with frost.
You walk fast to keep warm, and it does not help much.
A wind comes across the open country and leans on you the whole way.
Fog lies on the {way}, and things come out of it one at a time: a gate, a tree, a stone.
You leave {from} under a low lid of cloud that never quite comes to rain.
The sky is one grey from edge to edge, and the light is the same at every hour of the way.
The heat sits on the {way} like a weight, and you walk slower than you meant to.
Ash comes down soft as snow the whole way, and greys everything it settles on, you included.
You set out from {from} in the full of the afternoon, the {way} pale with dust.
You leave {from} late, with the light already going yellow.
The shadows are long when you leave {from}, and getting longer.
You go out of {from} into the dark, by what light there is.
You set out from {from}.
Partway, the {way} goes down to the water and through it, and up the far bank with your boots full.
The {way} follows the river a while, close enough to hear it, and crosses where it runs wide and shallow.
For a while the {way} runs along a shore, and birds get up off the water as you pass.
The {way} goes out across the fen on a raised bank, reed on either hand taller than a man, open water glinting through it.
Out on the fen the sky is enormous, and the only things standing up in all that flatness are you and a heron.
Water stands on both sides, and the {way} between is soft enough to take the print of your boot and keep it.
For an hour the {way} runs under trees, and the light comes down green and broken through the leaves.
The {way} goes into the wood, and the wood closes over it, and for a long time there is nothing to see but the next bend.
Somewhere in the wood someone is cutting timber; you hear the axe a long time and never see who.
The {way} runs between hedges and small fields, past a farm or two where dogs bark at you over the gate.
It is easy going through open country: a mill, a ford, a man ploughing who stops to watch you go by.
Larks go up out of the grass on either hand, and come down again behind you.
The {way} climbs onto open moor, and the country falls away behind you in long brown folds.
Up on the tops there is nothing but heather, sky and wind, and a cairn now and then to say you are still on the {way}.
The {way} goes up by stony steps and down by worse, and the wind finds you on every rise.
Sheep stand on the {way} and watch you come, as if you were the one who had strayed.
There are no trees up here, and after the first mile no walls: only the {way}, the sky, and the long backs of the hills.
The {way} climbs into the hills, switching back and forth on itself, until the land you came from is small below you.
The light goes before you are halfway, and you walk the rest by guess and by the pale line of the {way}.
Night comes on while you are still on the {way}. An owl keeps pace with you for a while, and then thinks better of it.
{to} shows ahead a long while before you reach it: smoke, a roofline, the noise of it on the wind.
The smoke of {to} comes up over the next rise, and then the roofs.
{to} is a handful of roofs at the end of the road, and a dog that comes out to see who you are.
It is a long walk, and your feet know it by the end.
By the end of it you are footsore, and glad of the sight of anywhere at all.
The last mile is the longest, as it always is.
